title: The "human" side of human resources
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Melissa Muth Martinez argues that HR as historically organised is a thing of the past because it lumps transactional work like payroll and compliance together with the human work of culture, trust and development. Citing MIT research, she says toxic culture, not pay, is the biggest driver of attrition, and that disrespect is the strongest predictor of how employees see culture. She illustrates with a 60-person organisation where one HR person was buried in paperwork and the result was a textbook toxic culture and high turnover. Her proposal is to keep compliance specialists and add dedicated leadership coaches, learning and development staff, mediators and community builders. The piece is more manifesto than practical guide, but the structural argument is clear.
points: Push factors, especially toxic culture, drive attrition more than pay or benefits.
Culture can be diagnosed by five elements, led by disrespect and lack of consideration.
One HR person handling all the transactional work cannot also build culture, and the result was predictable.
Organisations need separate transformational roles such as leadership coaches, mediators and community builders alongside compliance staff.
quotes: Push factors are the things happening internally that may prompt an employee to want to leave their role or the organization more broadly. Pay or benefits may be considerations, but research out of MIT shows that a toxic culture is often the biggest driver of workplace attrition.
It might be shocking to some, but research suggests that the latter often comes out on top. Sure, money’s nice, but alone, it’s usually not enough to keep us going.

The human side of a business is the one that relishes culture. It’s the one that invests in leadership, builds trust, mediates conflict, and not only pays attention to how people are doing, but how the work is functioning on a human level.
Not once did HR sponsor or lead a professional development initiative. Not once did they initiate a culture conversation or a pulse check. Not once did they ask, “How are things really going?
At the end of the day, the people are the business… they’re the heart and soul that turns our ability to do something into our ability to be something.

We need benefits, payroll, and compliance specialists, but we also need leadership coaches, learning and development staff, conflict and mediation experts, community builders, and other transformational roles.
